Supporting the walls: An excavation can be supported by sloping (without any structure), by shoring (the opposite soil faces are braced against each other), by embedded retaining walls – a wall with spaced reinforcement, a sheet pile wall, a pile wall or a diaphragm wall –, which in a deeper excavation are complemented by tie-backs or internal propping, by reinforcing the soil itself with nails, and finally by special solutions. Excavation support walls usually reach below the bottom of the excavation: their embedment provides one support through the passive earth resistance. As cantilevers – without other support – they are stable only for excavations of a few metres (max. 4–6 m). For a deeper excavation they have to be supported at one or more levels, which gives statically indeterminate continuous beams. The support can be of two kinds: a tie-back reaching behind the wall (ground anchor, passive tie-back) or internal propping placed in the excavation (steel pipe strut, propping slab).

The five steps of ground freezing
In the dry the anchor ends are fixed, and the final base slab and the structure are built on the underwater slab.
The water is pumped out gradually. From below the water pressure lifts the slab – it is held down by its own weight and the tensile force of the anchors.
Divers clean the anchor heads; the slab is concreted with tremie pipes, the end of the pipe staying in the fresh concrete all the time.
From a pontoon, tension piles (GEWI bars, micropiles) are drilled and grouted below the excavation bottom in a dense grid of 2,5–3,5 m.
The groundwater is not lowered: the soil is dredged from under water, and the excavation becomes an “artificial lake”.
the impermeable layer is deep down
A watertight sheet pile wall (or diaphragm wall) encloses the excavation – but it does not reach the deep impermeable layer.
The working space is flooded and the sheet piles are extracted; the concrete plug stays under the pier.
The water is pumped out, and the pier is built in the dry on the concrete plug.
An underwater concrete plug is placed with a tremie pipe: its weight resists the water pressure from below.
Inside the sheet pile wall the soil is removed under water with a grab, down to the design depth.
Along the frame – working from the middle in two directions – the sheet piles are driven all round.
From a barge guide piles are driven, and the bracing frame is fixed on them – this is the template for driving the sheet piles.
After the final structure is complete, the cooling is switched off and the ground slowly thaws.
Protected by the ice wall the ground is excavated and the face is covered with shotcrete; the freezing is maintained meanwhile.
The neighbouring ice cylinders grow together: a closed, watertight and load-bearing ice wall forms. Temperature pipes confirm it.
Brine at −30 °C (or liquid nitrogen at −196 °C) circulates in the pipes: the pore water freezes and ice cylinders grow around the pipes.
Along the outline of the excavation freeze pipes are drilled about every 1 m, down to the impermeable layer.
The nails “stitch” the soil together: the reinforced block works as a gravity wall. The nails must reach beyond the slip surface.
The next lift may be excavated only when the shotcrete is at least 72 hours old (or has reached about 10,5 MPa).
Reinforcing mesh is placed on the face, the nail heads are fixed, and the face is covered with 8–15 cm of shotcrete; a drainage mat goes behind it.
The nails are drilled (or driven) in at an inclination of 10–20° and grouted.
The soil is excavated in lifts of 1–2 m; for that time the soil face has to stand on its own.
Working downwards the intermediate slab and then the base slab are completed. For a building the superstructure can rise upwards at the same time.
Under the slab, in a confined space, small machines excavate; the soil is taken out through the opening. Meanwhile traffic on the surface is undisturbed.
After a shallow excavation the top slab is cast on the ground as formwork, with a muck opening. It props the walls as a diaphragm, and traffic can soon return.
From the surface the bored pile of the intermediate support is made, and the steel column is plunged into the fresh concrete.
First the perimeter diaphragm walls (or pile walls) are built from the surface.
The strut is removed only when the final structure (base slab, floor slab) already takes over the load.
Excavation continues below the struts; in a deep excavation further strut levels follow.
The pipe strut is preloaded with a hydraulic jack and fixed with steel wedges – so the wall moves less.
A steel waling is fixed to the walls, and the pipe strut is lifted in.
Once the walls are complete, the excavation is taken about 0,5 m below the planned strut level.
During excavation the wall moves a few centimetres, the rod is tensioned, and passive earth resistance develops in front of the anchor wall.
The trench is backfilled with sand, compacted in layers; the rod remains in the ground.
The rod is laid in a narrow trench 0,8–1,0 m below the surface and connected to the walings of the two walls. It is not prestressed: only the slack is taken up.
The main wall is driven, and outside the active wedge forming behind it the anchor wall (a driven I-section, a short sheet pile wall or a row of piles).
A reinforced concrete capping beam ties the pile heads together; keeping pace with the excavation, a waling beam and anchors (or struts) are installed.
The reinforcement cage is pushed into the freshly concreted secondary pile – these reinforced piles carry the bending moment.
After the final structure is complete, the excavation is backfilled and the sheet piles are extracted with a vibrator – they can be reused.
The sheets – mostly paired in the factory – are set in a guide frame so that the wall is straight and vertical.
First the primary and then the secondary panels cutting into them are made – so the wall is continuous and watertight.
Steel I/H sections are set into the fresh mix; the next primary panel can already be made.
The two pairs of counter-rotating wheels of the cutter head break up the soil on the way down while slurry is added.
No concrete goes into the trench: the slurry, containing cement, hardens by itself (single-phase method). Meanwhile the next panel is made.
Secondary columns are placed between the primary columns; the overlap closes the wall, making it quasi-watertight.
A steel I/H section is lowered into the still fluid column – into its axis, which the drill rod has passed through.
The small drilling rig sinks a hole of about 10–15 cm down to the bottom of the planned column.
At the edge the slab and the basement wall are completed; the raking strut can be removed only after that, once the basement structure is finished.
The berm is removed in sections, bay by bay, under the struts – in the other bays the soil still provides support.
The wall is propped onto the finished slab with a waling and raking steel struts. The vertical component of the strut force lifts the wall – the strut must be flat.
In the middle of the excavation – beyond the toe of the berm – the inner part of the base slab is built.
A sloping earth berm is left next to the wall, and the middle of the excavation is taken down to the final depth.
The box is pulled forward along the trench or lifted out section by section; behind it the trench is backfilled in compacted layers.
At the design depth the workers lay the pipe protected by the box.
Digging goes on inside the box, at most about 0,5 m ahead, then the box is pushed down with the bucket – the two alternate.
The excavator lifts the trench box on chains into the pre-excavated trench: two steel panels with adjustable struts between them.
Backfilling in compacted layers (15–20 cm); the struts are removed from the bottom up – a strut may come out only when there is soil supporting below it.
The pipe is lowered in the free space between the strut rows and laid on bedding. Walking or standing on the struts is forbidden.
The trench is deepened step by step, the planks are driven further down, and a new waling–strut row is installed.
The soil faces are covered with planks, held together by walings, and the walings are braced against each other with steel screw struts.
At first the trench is only taken down as far as the soil face will safely stand without support (m₀).
Below the locked-off anchor row excavation continues to below the next row – the cycle is repeated row by row down to the bottom.
The grout hardens in 8–12 days. Then the anchor is test-loaded with a jack and locked off at 80–90% of the design force.
The strands are pushed into the hole, the fixed length is grouted with cement grout and the casing is withdrawn; if necessary, post-grouting follows.
The anchor rig drills behind the wall at an inclination of 15–30°, protected by casing – even under the neighbouring plot.
Excavation may go only about 0,5 m below the level of the anchor row – no deeper until the anchor is working.
The planks are removed from the bottom up, keeping pace with the backfill compacted in layers; finally the beams are extracted – they can be reused.
Excavation and lagging proceed step by step, keeping pace with each other, down to the final excavation bottom.
After the secondary panel is reinforced and concreted, the panels form a continuous wall.
Between two finished primary panels the secondary panel is bitten out.
After the middle bite the primary panel stands open over its full length – under slurry.
